description: Somos AgroClyra, un equipo de tres estudiantes de Ingeniería Civil Industrial de la Universidad de La Frontera (UFRO), Temuco, Chile. Nos apasionan la innovación, la tecnología y la resolución de problemas reales. En el NASA Space Apps Challenge buscamos aplicar nuestros conocimientos en ingeniería, análisis de datos y desarrollo de soluciones tecnológicas para transformar información científica en herramientas útiles que contribuyan a un futuro más sostenible.
summary:
We developed AgroClyra, a Spanish-language Android and web prototype that helps farmers organize crop rotation planning. Farmers can map their land, record field activities, describe soil and water conditions, and prepare an editable three-season rotation plan. Traffic lights explain planning concerns and identify missing information.

AgroClyra integrates NASA POWER historical environmental data, NASA GIBS regional imagery, and NASA Earthdata CMR scene discovery. Separately identified providers supply weather forecasts and regional soil and solar information. The app also includes weather advisories and a visual PDF farm notebook.

By bringing farm records and environmental context together, AgroClyra aims to make rotation planning more accessible and support better-informed farming decisions. Version 0.6 demonstrates the workflow, while farmer trials and local agronomic validation remain future priorities.
details:
AgroClyra is a Spanish-language Android and web prototype that helps farmers organize field records and plan crop rotations. Version 0.6 brings farm information and environmental context into one application.

The farmer draws a farm boundary once and can edit it later. The same area becomes available to the notebook and rotation planning screens. Farmers describe their soil, water availability, known problems such as compaction or erosion, priorities and practical constraints. They can record agricultural activities and maintain a history of their crops.

AgroClyra compares crop options through explanatory traffic lights. Green identifies an option favorable to consider, orange highlights conditions requiring review, red indicates a rotation concern, and gray shows that information is missing. These indicators use planning rules rather than a certified crop suitability model. Farmers can also edit and save a three-season rotation proposal, which remains separate from completed sowing records.

NASA POWER provides historical daily environmental information, including temperature, precipitation, humidity, solar radiation and shallow soil temperature. NASA GIBS supplies dated satellite imagery for regional context. NASA Earthdata CMR supports ECOSTRESS and HLS scene discovery and metadata searches. Version 0.6 does not process those satellite rasters into field-level temperature measurements or vegetation indices. NASA SVS/LRO imagery also supports the lunar display, while the application approximates the phase locally.

Weather forecasts come from MET Norway. Open-Meteo/DWD ICON provides regional soil-temperature and solar forecasts. The application identifies these sources separately from NASA data. A notification bell presents in-app weather advisories, and farmers can view daily solar energy and a soil-temperature color map. The map represents regional model estimates rather than measurements within individual fields.

We developed the application using Flutter and Dart, with Sembast for local storage, Firebase Authentication for accounts, and Firestore for explicit user-controlled backups. PDF and KML exports help farmers share records and boundaries. An optional OpenRouter integration supports consent-based analysis of available farm context using a free-model route.

The project’s creative contribution is the combination of farmer-entered priorities, environmental information and explained planning rules in an accessible workflow. Our team considered usability, incomplete information, water constraints, soil problems and the distinction between historical data, forecasts and proposed actions.

AgroClyra aims to support clearer planning, better-informed timing of fieldwork and easier record sharing. These are intended benefits, not measured outcomes. Future work includes farmer trials, regional agronomic validation and quality-controlled satellite analysis.
